blocks.md:
**있어요** = it exists / there is / I have.
**없어요** = it does not exist / there is none / I don’t have.

One pair of words, three English translations. Korean does not separate *having* from *existing*.

items.tip: Do you have time? — literally “time exists?”

blocks.md: **없어요 is not 안 + 있어요.** Korean has a separate word for the negative here, and 안 있어요 is simply not said. Learn the pair together as one item.

blocks.h: The thing that exists takes 이/가
blocks.md:
돈**이** 없어요.  ·  시간**이** 있어요.

Same consonant/vowel split you already know.

blocks.q: “I have no money.” — 돈 ends in ㄴ, a consonant.
blocks.why: 돈 ends in a consonant → **이**. 돈가 uses the vowel form; 안 있어요 is not said in Korean — the negative word is 없어요; 을 marks an object, but 없어요 takes a subject.
없어요 is the “there is none / I don’t have” half of the pair.

blocks.q: “Do you have time?”  시간 ___?
blocks.why: 있어요 with a rising intonation is the question. Korean does not reorder words to ask.

blocks.meaning: There is a book in the bag.
blocks.why: Something existing somewhere → **있어요**. 없어요 is the opposite; 이에요 says what a thing *is*; 아니에요 says what it is not.

blocks.q: Which is the correct way to say “I don’t have a younger sibling”?
blocks.why: The negative of 있어요 is the separate word **없어요** — 안 있어요 is not said. 을 is the object tag, and 아니에요 would mean “it is not a younger sibling”.

blocks.q: Build “Where is the bathroom?”
Write it yourself: **“I have no money.”**  (money = 돈)
blocks.hint: The thing that does not exist takes 이/가 — and 돈 ends in a consonant.
blocks.why: 돈이 없어요. Adding 저는 at the front is fine and slightly more explicit.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “I am at home right now.”

title: Lesson 2. 에 or 에서? Look at the verb

blocks.md:
English uses *at* for both of these:

I am **at** home.  ·  I study **at** home.

Korean does not. It uses **에** for the first and **에서** for the second — and the choice is decided by **the verb**, not by the place.

head: Use
When
Example
rows: 집**에** 있어요 — I am at home
집**에서** 공부해요 — I study at home

blocks.md:
The test that always works: **ask what the verb is doing.**

있다 · 없다 · 살다 · 가다 · 오다 → the place is a **location or destination** → **에**
anything you *do* (먹다, 공부하다, 일하다, 만나다) → the place is a **stage for the action** → **에서**

items.tip: I am at home. 있다 → 에
I study at home. 공부하다 → 에서
I go to school. 가다 is a destination → 에
I meet a friend at school. 만나다 → 에서

blocks.q: “I eat at the restaurant.”  식당___ 먹어요
blocks.why: 먹다 is an action, so the restaurant is where it **happens** → **에서**. **에** would be for being or going there (식당에 가요); **은** marks a topic and **이** a subject.

blocks.meaning: I am at home right now.
blocks.why: 있다 asks *where something is*, so it takes **에**. **에서** would be for an action done there, **은** marks a topic, **으로** means toward or by means of.

blocks.meaning: I work at the company every day.
blocks.why: 일하다 is something you **do**, so the place is a stage → **에서**. **에** marks location or destination, **까지** means “up to”, **도** means “also”.

blocks.q: Match each verb with the particle its place takes.

blocks.why: 가다 has a destination, not a stage → **에**. **에서** would be for something you *do* at school, **을** is the object tag, **도** means “also”.

blocks.q: Both are real sentences. Which one means “I **study** at the library”?
blocks.why: Studying is an action → **에서**. 도서관에 있어요 means “I am at the library”, 도서관에 가요 means “I go to the library”, and 도서관이에요 means “it is a library”.

blocks.q: Write it yourself: **“I work at home.”**  (work = 일하다, home = 집)
blocks.hint: Working is something you *do*, so which one — 에 or 에서? And 하다 becomes 해요.
blocks.why: 집에서 일해요. 집에 일해요 would be the classic mistake — 에 marks where something *is*, not where it happens.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “I study at home.”

blocks.md:
The same **에** also marks **when** something happens.

세 시**에** 만나요.  — Let’s meet at three.
월요일**에** 가요.  — I go on Monday.

**A few time words refuse 에.** 오늘 · 어제 · 내일 · 지금 · 매일 take no particle at all.

내일 만나요.  (○)
내일에 만나요.  (✗)

There is no rule to derive here — these are simply the common ones, and they are common enough that you will absorb them fast.

items.tip: I drink coffee in the morning.
What do you do on the weekend?
I go to school tomorrow. 내일 takes no 에 — but 학교 does.

blocks.q: Which sentence is wrong?
blocks.why: 내일 is one of the time words that take **no particle** — 내일 만나요. 일요일, 아침 and 세 시 all take **에** normally.
A clock time takes **에**. **에서** is for places where actions happen, **부터** means “from”, **까지** means “until”.
내일 is one of the time words that take **no particle**. 내일에 adds one it refuses; 아침에는 means “in the morning”; 내일이 marks it as a subject.

blocks.q: Which of these time words takes **에**?
blocks.why: 주말**에** 쉬어요. 오늘, 지금 and 매일 all take no particle — 오늘 바빠요, 지금 가요, 매일 운동해요.

blocks.q: “I drink coffee in the morning.”  아침___ 커피를 마셔요
blocks.why: 아침 is a time → 에.

blocks.q: Write it yourself: **“Let’s meet at seven.”**  (seven o’clock = 일곱 시)
blocks.hint: A clock time takes 에. And remember 만나요 does the inviting all by itself.
blocks.why: 일곱 시에 만나요. The plain 해요 form said warmly is the everyday way to suggest something — no extra word needed.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “Let’s meet at seven.”

title.ko: 4강. 이/가 있어요와 없어요 — 명사 뒤에 바르게 붙이기
title.en: Lesson 4. Forming 있어요 and 없어요 — Picking the Right Particles

blocks.md:
When you say what exists or what you have, the item takes **이** or **가** before **있어요** or **없어요**.

• Consonant ending (받침): noun + **이 있어요 / 없어요**
• Vowel ending (no 받침): noun + **가 있어요 / 없어요**

To add a location, mark the place with **에**:

• **가방에** 열쇠가 있어요. (There is a key in the bag.)
• **집에** 우산이 없어요. (There is no umbrella at home.)

items.tip: I don’t have cash in my wallet right now. (현금 = cash, 지갑 = wallet)
There is a small desk in the room.
I have an important appointment this afternoon.

blocks.q: Choose the correct sentence for “I have an umbrella.” (우산 = umbrella)
blocks.why: **우산** ends in the consonant ㄴ (받침), so it takes the subject particle **이** → **우산이 있어요**.

blocks.meaning: I don't have a car right now, so I take the subway.
blocks.why: **차** (car) ends in a vowel (no 받침), so it takes **가** → **차가 없어요**.

blocks.q: Match each noun to its correct pattern with 있어요.
“Do you have a pen (펜)?” Complete the question: 펜___ 있어요?
blocks.why: **펜** ends in the consonant ㄴ (받침), so it takes the subject marker **이**.

blocks.q: Put the words in order: “There is an umbrella at home.”
Say it out loud: “There is a wallet in the bag.”
